title: Sherring v. Canada (Attorney General)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicant = BRENDA SHERRING; respondent = ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: Brenda Sherring was denied “taxpayer relief” from penalties and interest for late-filed taxes. She seeks judicial review of the October 25, 2023, second review refusal, which she says failed to account for her financial situation. Unfortunately, while Ms. Sherring may have a good case for entering into a payment plan that reflects her current circumstances, she has not persuaded me that the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) acted unreasonably in refusing to grant her relief from the penalties and interest she owes.

Ms. Sherring is a 71-year-old English language instructor living in Saskatchewan. She did not file her 2011 – 2016 personal tax returns on time, and as a result, the CRA issued notices of tax assessment in 2018 that included arears interest and filing penalties for those years. Although she subsequently filed tax returns for the 2013-2016 tax years, which resulted in the CRA issuing amended notices of assessment, the penalties and arears interest amounts remained unchanged.
Ms. Sherring again filed her tax returns late for the 2017 and 2019 tax years. The CRA again issued notices of assessment that included arrears interest and late filing penalties.

In April 2022, Ms. Sherring requested relief from penalties and interest owing in respect of the 2006 through 2021 tax years. The request was made pursuant to subsection 220(3.1) of the Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp) which grants the Minister discretionary authority to provide relief from tax penalties and interest. Ms. Sherring based her request on what she said were her financial hardship, medical problems and COVID-19.

The CRA denied the request. The decision maker noted that the CRA could only consider relief of penalties and interest accrued in the 10 years before the request was made (thus excluding tax years 2006-2010) and observed that there were no penalties or interest related to the 2007-2009 tax years. As for the 2011-2021 tax years, the CRA found that Ms. Sherring had not been prevented from meeting her filing and remitting obligations and relief was therefore not warranted.

Ms. Sherring requested a second review of her request for relief from interest and penalties related to the 2011-2021 tax years. She based her request on her financial hardship, illness and emotional and mental distress, and she supported it with a letter, written representations and medical documentation regarding a leg fracture that occurred in 2019.

The CRA decision maker who conducted the second review again refused Ms. Sherring’s tax relief request. The decision maker observed that by Ms. Sherring’s own admission she had not spoken with a doctor about her mental health issues and therefore had no documentation to support her claim. The decision maker further noted that according to the evidence Ms. Sherring’s leg fracture occurred on June 1, 2019, and was healed by October 2, 2019. The decision maker found that the 2019 leg injury had no bearing on Ms. Sherring’s ability to comply with her tax obligations for the eight preceding tax years.

As for Ms. Sherring’s assertion of financial difficulties, the decision maker explained that in the relief context, financial hardship involves a “prolonged inability to provide necessities,” and requires an “extraordinary circumstance” preventing a taxpayer from filing and/or paying taxes on time. The evidence before the CRA showed that Ms. Sherring had funded renovations for two houses, sold a house, paid off a line of credit, bought a car, and contributed over $70,000 to her Registered Retirement Savings Plan accounts between 2019-2022. Based on this evidence, the decision maker found that Ms. Sherring was not experiencing financial hardship and was not prevented from meeting her filing obligations due to circumstances beyond her own control.

Ms. Sherring seeks judicial review of this second review decision. She alleges that the CRA misunderstood her financial circumstances and failed to consider her age, physical limitation and ability to continue employment.

The standard of review applicable to the CRA second reviewer’s decision is reasonableness. A reasonable decision is one that is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 85 [Vavilov]). To be reasonable, an administrative decision must be justified, intelligible and transparent (Vavilov at para 99). It must reflect the evidence.

During the hearing of this judicial review, Ms. Sherring spoke at length about the obstacles she has faced over the years, including financial, physical, and emotional challenges. I sympathize with Ms. Sherring. However, as I explained during the hearing, my role as a reviewing judge is to examine the decision of the CRA in light of the record that was before it. Unless the decision is unreasonable based on that record, or was reached in a procedurally unfair way, I cannot interfere with it, even if I might have weighed the evidence differently.

Ms. Sherring has not persuaded me that the CRA second review decision was unreasonable. The decision maker engaged with the submissions, reviewed the evidence, and came to a clearly articulated, rational conclusion that reflected the scope of discretion available under the law. There is no valid basis upon which to disturb the CRA’s decision.

While I must therefore dismiss this application, I note that as acknowledged by counsel for the Respondent, it remains open to Ms. Sherring to put her full circumstances, properly supported by evidence, before the CRA in support of a request to negotiate a workable payment plan that reflects her present financial situation.
The Respondent’s request for costs is dismissed in light of Ms. Sherring’s circumstances.

Finally, the Respondent notes that Ms. Sherring, who is not represented by counsel, has named the incorrect party as the Respondent in this matter. I agree. Pursuant to Rule 303 of the Federal Courts Rules, SOR/98-106, the Attorney General of Canada should be named as the Respondent. The style of cause shall be amended accordingly. JUDGMENT in T-2564-23 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The style of cause is amended to identify the Attorney General of Canada as the Respondent. The application is dismissed. The parties are responsible for their own costs. "Andrew J. Brouwer" Judge FEDERAL COURT SOLICITORS OF RECORD Docket: T-2564-23 STYLE OF CAUSE: BRENDA SHERRING v.
